subject: Copywriting
title: The Committee on Public Information
description: A quick win: understand The Committee on Public Information.

hook.text: In 1917, President Wilson created the CPI—a government propaganda machine that turned pacifist America warlike.

buildup.text: George Creel led the CPI. He recruited writers, artists, and filmmakers to produce posters, pamphlets, and newsreels.

discovery.text: The CPI deployed '4-Minute Men'—75,000 volunteers giving 4-minute speeches in movie theaters before films.

twist.text: The CPI demonized Germans with fabricated atrocity stories.

climax.text: After the war, Americans learned many stories were lies. The CPI created lasting distrust of government messaging.

punchline.text: 75,000 speakers, every theater. The US government industrialized propaganda.

quiz.question: What were the '4-Minute Men'?
options: Volunteers who gave 4-minute speeches in theaters

details.summary: The Committee on Public Information, created by Woodrow Wilson in 1917, was America's first official propaganda agency. Led by George Creel, it used posters, films, and a network of 75,000 volunteer speakers called 'Four Minute Men' to build support for World War I.
details.whyItMatters: The CPI demonstrated that democratic governments also use propaganda. Its methods — combining mass media, grassroots networks, and emotional appeals — became the model for government communication campaigns worldwide.
takeaways: The CPI was America's first systematic propaganda operation
The Four Minute Men delivered propaganda as community speeches
Government propaganda can exist in democratic societies, not just authoritarian ones

faq.question: What were the Four Minute Men?
faq.answer: A network of 75,000 volunteers who delivered scripted four-minute speeches in movie theaters, churches, and public gatherings. They personalized government messaging at a local level, making propaganda feel like community conversation rather than top-down instruction.

faq.question: Why was the Committee dissolved after the war?
faq.answer: Congress shut it down in 1919 amid concerns about government overreach in shaping public opinion. The CPI's effectiveness actually alarmed many Americans, sparking debates about propaganda in democracies that continue today.
